en: Hi everyone. Today I want to talk about imagination and theater. For the past year, I've been playing "Matilda" at the Cambridge Theatre in London's West End. The theater has 1,249 seats and it is almost full every single night. "Matilda" is based on the book by Roald Dahl, and a lot of you probably already know the story. It is about a brave little girl who, even though she is bullied by her parents, uses her intelligence, courage and magic to take control of her own life.

Well I am that Matilda alongside three other amazing girls. The four of us share the lead role, which is wonderful, but getting here was not exactly simple. I had to go through six rounds of auditions twice. The first time was in spring 2024. I made it all the way to the final round, but then got a really bad cold. I couldn't sing, I couldn't perform. So I had to stop. Six months later, I had to go through the whole process all over again. And then came the hardest part. The waiting. Four whole weeks of not knowing. It felt like four years. But then finally, one day, the call came. I'd been offered the role. I didn't know whether to laugh or cry. So I did both at the same time.

Here's something I should tell you, though. "Matilda" and I go way back. Long before auditions. Long before any of this. I started watching the 1996 "Matilda" film when I was just three years old. I watched it over and over again. I would sit very still, staring at objects around the house and trying to make them wobble. So when I finally got to step onto the real stage at the Cambridge Theatre, I could do things with my eyes -- well after seven years of staring at cups.

Three months of intensive rehearsals followed. Every step, every line, every move, again and again until I didn't have to think about it anymore. The cast and coaches were all so patient with me. Honestly, they deserved medals. But somewhere in all those hours, something had changed. I'd stopped trying to find Matilda because I realized she'd been inside me the whole time. She was the girl I'd been dreaming about since I was three. I didn't become her. I just finally let her out.

The theater itself is a world of its own. It has lights, painted walls, window frames, desks and swings. And there is a library where I can dive into my books and find the wonderful Mrs. Phelps waiting for me. There is my very kind Miss Honey, and over there, sitting in front of the telly with my brother are my rather obnoxious parents, and somewhere, lurking in the shadows, is the terrifying Miss Trunchbull. Every night before the show starts, I stand backstage, getting ready. In my mind, I think about Matilda's life, her love of books, her hatred of bullies, her courage to find her own way to fight back. I breathe in, I breathe out, and then I step onto the stage. And when I'm in the light, I am her. I’m brave enough to stand up to Miss Trunchbull when she grabs [a] boy by his ears. I shout to her with everything I have. My heart beats so fast, I can feel it. When my dad rips my books, I know I'm resilient and that I will get my own back. Glue his hat to his head, dye his hair green. Every time, I have any smile right here. I love standing on [an] elevated bookstand during quiet. Everything's so still, so quiet. But my heart is pounding as I feel all [of] Matilda’s anger bursting out through my eyes.

But things in life do not always go as planned. And the same is true on stage. One night during the scene where I hug Miss Honey, because she’d offered me something no one else ever has: kindness, I hug her very tightly. At that exact moment, Miss Trunchbull ran in. We were supposed to spring apart, except we couldn't because my hair was completely tangled into her necklace. One second, two seconds. Five seconds of stage time feels rather long, let me tell you. But nobody panicked. We stayed calm. We stayed in the scene. Quietly, very quietly, we untangled ourselves. I lost some hair and Miss Honey lost a necklace, but we carried on. The audience never noticed a thing, and most luckily, Miss Trunchbull didn't catch us either. You see, the stage and life are not so different because imagination isn't about escaping the real world. It is a way of building one. And when our imaginations work together, every character on that stage comes alive. The cast, the crew, and every single person in the audience all join in. That is when the real magic happens. I look out and see your shining faces back at me. I can see smiles, I can see tears. I hear you clapping so hard as if you'd never want to leave Matilda's world. And honestly, neither do I. But at that moment, I want to give every single one of you the biggest hug and tell you, Matilda loves you all.
Thank you.
(Applause)
zh: 大家好。 今天我想谈谈想象力和戏剧。 在过去的一年里， 我一直在伦敦西区的剑桥剧院 参演《玛蒂尔达》。 剧院有 1,249 个座位， 几乎每晚都座无虚席。 《玛蒂尔达》改编自 罗尔德 · 达尔的书， 可能很多人早就听过这个故事了。 这是关于一个勇敢的小女孩， 尽管深受父母虐待，却凭借智慧、 勇气与魔法，重新掌握了 自己的人生的故事。

没错，我就是玛蒂尔达的扮演者之一， 另外还有三位了不起的女孩们 我们四个人共同扮演主角。 这很棒，不过一路走来 一点都不轻松。 我参加了两次六轮的试镜。 第一次是在 2024 年春季 我一路进入了最后一轮， 但随后感冒得非常严重。 我无法唱歌，也无法表演 所以我必须停下来。 六个月后， 我不得不重新经历整个过程 然后是最难的部分： 等待。 整整四周的不知情 漫长得如同过去了四年。 但是终于，有一天，电话来了 我被邀请担任这个角色。 我不知道该笑还是该哭 所以我两件事同时都做了。
不过，我应该告诉你一件事。 我与《玛蒂尔达》早就相识了。 早在试镜前。 早在这一切之前。 我三岁时就开始看 1996 年的 《玛蒂尔达》电影。 我一遍又一遍地看。 我会静静地坐着， 盯着房子周围的物体想让它们摇晃。 因此，当我终于踏上 剑桥剧院的真实舞台时， 我可以用眼睛做事—— 在盯着杯子看了七年之后。
随后进行了三个月的密集排练 每步、每行、每一个动作， 一次又一次，直到它 成为了本能反应。 演员和教练都对我非常耐心。 老实说，应该为他们颁个奖。 但是在所有这些时间里， 情况发生了变化。 我已经停止寻找玛蒂尔达了， 因为我意识到她一直在我体内。 她是我从三岁起就梦寐以求的女孩。 我没有成为她。 相反，我把她放出来了。

剧院本身就是一个自己的世界。 它有灯光、彩绘墙壁、 窗框、书桌和秋千。 那里还有一座图书馆， 我可以沉浸在书海中， 并发现超棒的 菲尔普斯夫人正在等我。 还有我非常善良的哈尼小姐， 在那边，和我哥哥一起坐在电视机前的 是我相当讨厌的父母， 而潜伏在阴影中的某个地方是 可怕的特伦奇布尔小姐。 每天晚上，在演出开始之前， 我都会站在后台做好准备。 我脑海中浮现出玛蒂尔达的一生， 她对书籍的热爱，对恶霸的仇恨， 她寻找自己的反击方式的勇气。 我吸气，呼气， 然后踏上舞台。 当我在灯光下时，我就是她。 当特伦奇布尔小姐抓住 一位男孩的耳朵时， 我勇敢地挺身而出。 我尽自己所能向她大喊大叫。 我能感觉到我的心跳得那么快。 当我爸撕掉我的书时， 我知道我有韧性， 而且我会把自己的书拿回来。 把他的帽子粘他头上， 把他的头发染成绿色。 每次，我都会在这里露出笑容 我喜欢在安静的时候站在架起的书架上 一切都那么安静，太安静了。 但是，我的心跳在加速， 随着我感觉到玛蒂尔达的所有愤怒 都在我的眼中爆发。

但是生活中的事情并不总按计划进行。 舞台上也是如此。 某晚演到我拥抱哈尼小姐那场戏， 因为她给了我别人 从未给过我的善意， 我紧紧地了拥抱她。 就在那一刻，特兰奇布尔小姐跑进来了 我们本该即刻分开的， 但我们不能， 因为我的头发完全缠在了她的项链上。 一秒钟，两秒钟。 让我告诉你， 五秒钟的舞台时间感觉很长。 但没有人惊慌。 我们保持冷静。我们一直没出戏 我们悄悄地，非常安静地 解开了自己的困境。 我掉了一些头发， 哈尼小姐丢了一条项链， 但我们仍然继续着。 观众没有注意到任何异常。 最幸运的是， 特兰奇布尔小姐 也没注意到我们。 你看，舞台和生活没有太大区别， 因为想象力不是要逃离现实世界。 它是一种建造方式。 当我们的想象力共同发挥作用时， 那个舞台上的每个角色都会活起来。 演员、工作人员和观众中的每一个人 都加入了。 那是真正的魔法发生的时候。 我往外看，看见你们容光焕发地朝向我。 我能看到笑容，我能看到眼泪。 我听到你们大声鼓掌， 仿佛不愿从玛蒂尔达的 世界抽离一般。 说实话，我也是。 但是那一刻，我想给你们每个人 一个最大的拥抱 然后告诉你们，玛蒂尔达爱你们。

en: To coincide with the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Japan launched the world’s first high-speed train, the Shinkansen. Capable of running at 210 kph, this groundbreaking bullet train inspired countries around the world to invest in high-speed rail. Today, these trains regularly travel at over 300 kph, on par with the takeoff speed of a commercial airplane. But could these trains go even faster, whisking passengers to their destinations quicker than the smoothest flight?

To answer this, it helps to understand how these trains reach their already impressive speeds. There are three main factors that separate bullet trains from traditional, low-speed trains: engines, aerodynamics, and infrastructure.

Most traditional trains are powered by combustion engines, which combust fuel— typically diesel— to turn an electric generator. This electricity is then used to power motors that turn the train’s wheels. High-speed trains, on the other hand, use electric engines to power their motors. This process is more energy efficient than combustion and allows train operators to reach top speeds more quickly.

Next up is aerodynamics. While low- and high-speed trains use the same steel wheels to minimize friction with the track, bullet trains are also designed with aerodynamic bodies that slice through air with minimal resistance. Engineers could use these slicker designs on traditional train cars. But while upgrading to electric engines would make low-speed trains more efficient, they wouldn't get much benefit from these aerodynamic designs because of the third factor: infrastructure.

Traditional train tracks were built to meet people where they lived, ensuring stations were accessible to any potential passengers. But to prevent derailments in these highly populated areas, trains need to frequently decelerate to safely hit turns and cross roads. High-speed rails, on the other hand, were built to prioritize speed. They run on long, straight lines that avoid road crossings, sharp curves, and high traffic areas. These three differences allow high-speed trains to reach top speeds over double their traditional counterparts. And since their infrastructure allows them to travel longer distances between stops, they spend more time cruising near top speed, often traveling up to three times the average speed of traditional trains. But new technology is emerging to make even faster trains.

To eliminate friction between rails and wheels, engineers have developed new magnetic levitation, or maglev, trains. There are two major approaches here. In electromagnetic suspension, magnetized arms wrap under the track and pull the train up. Meanwhile, in electrodynamic suspension, coils embedded in the track create a pattern of alternating magnetic fields that interact with magnets on the train to float the vehicle a few centimeters in the air. To change speed, train operators alternate the direction of the trains’ magnetic field, attracting the front of the train to the next coil to speed up or reversing the field’s phase to brake. Given enough runway, these trains can reach speeds from 430 to a theoretical 600 kph, allowing them to make the over 4,400 kilometer trip from New York City to Los Angeles in as little as seven hours. So why haven’t we built maglev trains, or even high-speed trains, everywhere?

First, these trains require lots of energy, most of which is needed to overcome air resistance. In fact, at 300 kph, this task accounts for over 80% of a train’s energy consumption. Engineers are researching ways to reduce air resistance, such as putting maglevs in near-vacuum environments. But building a vacuum-sealed tunnel across an entire country would be an infrastructure project of science fictional proportions. Besides, it’s hard enough to build regular high-speed rails. To go fast, trains need long, straight tracks with wide curves, which are very difficult to build in mountains, cities, or densely populated areas. Building such routes is costly, politically sensitive, and often physically impossible.

Despite these hurdles, Japan and China are expanding their existing high-speed and maglev rails, and several projects currently in development might finally bring high-speed rail to the US. But we’ll need to carefully consider our trains’ top speeds alongside cost, energy use, and safety to keep the future of train travel on the right track.
zh: 为了配合 1964 年东京奥运会， 日本推出了世界上 第一款高速列车——新干线。 这种极具开创性的子弹头列车 能以每小时 210 公里的速度运行， 激发了世界各国投资高速铁路。 如今，这些列车的行驶速度 通常超过时速 300 公里， 与商用飞机的起飞速度相当。 但是，这些列车还能更快吗？ 能比最平稳的航班 更快地将旅客发送到目的地吗？
要回答这个问题，我们得了解 列车如何达到这已经十分惊人的速度。 子弹头列车与传统低速列车的 主要区别有三个： 发动机、空气动力学和基础设施。
大多数传统列车都由内燃机提供动力。 内燃机通过燃烧燃料 （通常是柴油）来启动发电机。 然后，这些电力被用来 为转动火车轮的电机提供动力。 然而，高速列车 使用电动发动机来为发动机提供动力。 该过程比燃烧燃料更节能， 也能让列车驾驶员更快地提到最高速度。
然后是空气动力学。 虽然低速和高速列车使用相同的钢轮， 最大限度地减少与轨道的摩擦， 但子弹头列车的设计 还采用了空气动力学车体， 可以以最小的阻力穿过空气。 工程师可以在传统的火车车厢上 采用这些更流畅的设计。 但是，尽管升级成电动发动机 可以提高低速列车的效率， 但由于第三个因素——基础设施， 空气动力学设计帮不上太多忙。

传统的火车轨道是为了 迎合人们的居住地而建造的， 从而确保任何潜在乘客都能进入车站。 但是，为了防止 在这些人口密集的地区脱轨， 火车需要经常减速才能 安全地转弯、穿过十字路口。 另一方面，高速列车 就是为了速度设计的， 它们沿着长直线行驶，避开交叉路口、 急转弯道和交通繁忙的区域。 这三个差异使高速列车 能够达到最高速度 超过传统列车的两倍。 而且由于配套设施 让它可以有更长的站间距离， 它能更久地以接近最高的速度巡航， 行驶速度通常是 传统列车平均速度的三倍。 但还有新技术能让火车更快。

为了消除轨道和车轮之间的摩擦， 工程师们开发了 新型磁悬浮，或称“磁浮列车”。 这主要有两种作用。 电磁悬浮模式下， 励磁悬浮臂抱合于轨下， 将列车抬升至悬浮状态。 而在电动悬浮模式下， 嵌入轨道中的线圈 会产生一种交替磁场的模式， 与火车上的磁体相互作用， 使车辆在空中漂浮几厘米。 列车驾驶员通过改变 列车磁场方向改变速度， 将列车头推进到下一线圈加速， 逆转磁场的相位来制动。 如果有足够长的跑道， 这些列车的速度可以达到 时速 430 公里， 甚至是理论上的时速 600 公里， 使它们能够在短短七小时内完成 从纽约市到洛杉矶 超过 4,400 公里的行程。 那么，为什么我们没有四处 建造磁悬浮列车，甚至高速列车呢？

首先，这些列车需要大量能量， 大部分用于克服空气阻力。 例如，在每小时 300 公里的速度下， 这项用途占列车能耗的 80% 以上。 工程师们正在研究减少空气阻力的方法， 例如将磁悬浮列车置于近真空环境中。 但是，修建一条 横跨整个国家的真空密封隧道 将是一项科幻级别的基础设施项目。 此外，建造普通的高铁已经够困难了。 为了快速行驶， 列车需要长而直的轨道、宽弯道， 而在山区、城市或人口密集地区 很难修建这些轨道。 修建这样的路线 既昂贵又在政治上比较敏感， 现实情况几乎不可能实现。
尽管存在这些障碍， 日本和中国正在扩建 其现有的高速和磁悬浮铁路， 目前正在开发的几个项目 最终可能会将高铁带到美国。 但是，我们需要认真考虑列车的最高速度 以及成本、能源消耗和安全性， 保证未来的铁路旅行跑在正轨。

Thank you so much and hello everyone. I am 18 years old, and I am from Eugene, Oregon. I've been playing the accordion for about 12 years, and it is such a pleasure to be here and to share the beauty and versatility of my instrument with all of you. Recently, I had the privilege of performing for NPR's Tiny Desk Concerts. Thank you.
(Applause)

And there, I performed the piece that I have just played for you, called "The Prelude and Fugue" by one of my favorite classical composers, Johann Sebastian Bach. Now I love playing music in many different styles, from Bach to [The] Beatles to AC/DC -- especially in a duet with my father. He is my teacher and a professional accordion player himself.

Now before I play my final piece for you, I'd like to briefly familiarize you with this instrument. So this is a professional model of a B-system, chromatic button accordion, which has 120 buttons on the left side and only 106 on the right side. Not that many. There are also registers over here, which I use to change the tone of the sound, so I can imitate other instruments such as the bassoon, the piccolo, the organ and so on. And they are also duplicated up here. And these are called chin switches, which, as you can guess, I can operate using my chin, like this. And additionally, this middle part here, which I constantly push and pull, is called the bellows. And the bellows act as the lungs of the accordion since they pump air in and out and control the dynamics. Now considering this instrument weighs about 35 pounds, I would say it's a bit of a workout, as well as an intense brain exercise to handle. And you may be wondering why I chose to play such a unique instrument.

Well when I was little, we actually had this tiny little accordion in our living room, and one day I just came up to my dad and said, "Hey, can you teach me how to play this?" So I started off by learning a few chords and simple melodies, and I just fell in love with the instrument, even though the first-ever accordion I played didn't even have all the notes. So I would say that having a teacher at home living with me also helped me progress pretty quickly, which has brought me to where I am today. And now I would like to play for you "Moments Musicaux" by composer Franz Schubert.
(Applause)
(Music)
(Music ends)
(Applause and cheers)
Cloe Shasha Brooks: Salehe, thank you so much for joining us.
Salehe Bembury: Thanks for having me.

CSB: Among many of your popular designs, you made Crocs cool. And this is called the Crocs Pollex clog, based on your own fingerprint mold. And what I love is that Crocs reach out to you asking if they could send you some shoes. And you said, "How about we actually collaborate instead?" And they said yes. So once they said yes, how did you decide to do this specifically?

SB: It was a great honor because they first wanted to collaborate. And then when I sent them what I didn’t know was a kid’s Croc shoe, they let me know that they loved that I was thinking of the form of the Croc, which a lot of collaborators in the past were simply reskinning the Croc, maybe adding jibbitz. And I was thinking of the form, and that comes from my industrial-design background. Once they saw that I was interested in manipulating the form, they asked me if I wanted to be the first collaborative designer to create a Croc from scratch, which I immediately did a Birdman hand rub and said yes.
(Laughter)

And so this is the result of that. Initially I had to make sure that I fostered and maintained the existing elements of the Croc DNA and made sure that I didn't scare away the existing consumer and getting the honor of working with a brand like Crocs, you get to work with their heritage and their DNA. So I had to make sure to maintain that and then also introduce my own brand identity, put it through a new lens, and potentially speak to a new audience.

CSB: You know, it's pretty amazing because you've had a really amazing journey as a footwear designer. You started at Payless in 2009, and then you started doing collaborations with a lot of brands like New Balance, Cole Haan, Versace, to name a few. And now you run your own brand called Spunge, that's what those are. So to help paint the picture of how you've forged your own path, I'd love for you to share the story that I just love, of you being on your couch, eating cereal in a moment of unemployment and you somehow went from scrolling on LinkedIn to convincing Versace to give you your dream job. Will you tell us that story?

SB: So, cereal on my couch, that is a description of the image of unemployment that I was experiencing at that time. I was using all of the tools that have been given to us for outreach, LinkedIn, Craigslist, maybe it was even Facebook at the time, and sending messages to whoever would accept them. I reached out to a Versace design director, and I proposed an opportunity. I said, the sneaker industry is a multibillion-dollar business, and traditionally, that consumer isn't paying attention to fashion brands or traditionally paying attention to the sneaker brands that we're all used to and probably wearing right now. But then there was this mass education that happened that Raf Simons, Adidas, Nike, Comme des Garçons, and now this massive consumer was aware of the fact that fashion houses can make sneakers. And so I reached out to them, a few days later, Donatella herself responded. She said she loved my ideas. Perfect timing for that photo. She said that she wanted me to come out to Milan and present to her what I thought the sneaker program could be. I went out to Milan a few days later, presented a combination of merchandising and design and sales insight, and she loved it. And she was like, "I want to hire you. I want you to move to Milan right away. Do you want to consult?" She was really open about what the opportunity could be. Because she was so open, I asked if I could have my own design studio in Los Angeles and travel to Milan monthly for factory visits and shows and she said yes. So I went outside and did my pursuit of happiness -- cry in the streets -- because my life changed instantly. But really what that was more about was the power of asking and what that can bring you.
(Applause)

CSB: So throughout your career, you've always used color and form and function in a way that's felt really playful. There's so many nuanced details in your designs, like there's so many Easter eggs that people could find if they know what to look for. So I'm going to show some pictures of your shoes, and I'd love to hear you share your design philosophy for each of them. Tell us about these.

SB: So this was my first-ever collaboration with a Chinese brand called Anta. This was a from-scratch collaboration. A lot of collaborations these days are color-ups and skinings, but this was, I guess the result of a white piece of paper. And I guess what I was trying to accomplish here was an introduction to footwear, the footwear industry and the audience -- because before that I was working at different brands, and this was the first time that a piece of footwear was going to feature my name. So there was a lot of things that I had to introduce to my existing audience.
CSB: How about this one?

SB: This is the HALI 1. It's the first signature sneaker of Tyrese Haliburton. I became a footwear designer because of basketball. That was my kind of initial inspiration that made me feel the emotions that I believe I'm giving to others now. It is with Puma. He recently wore it in the previous NBA finals. It had a pretty tragic ending, but it was still amazing to be a part of that shoe and for it to fall at that part of my career was really special.
CSB: I love these.

SB: This was a shoe I did with Pyer Moss, which is a high-fashion brand. (Applause and cheers) Thank you very much, everybody. Isn't that a beautiful song? I just love it. You know, music is a language you already know. And there's something deeply powerful that happens when we come together to make it. Something connective, something transformative, something vibrational. It's a feeling that moves us. Now I have a name for this feeling. I call it the wiggle.
(Laughter)

Now what’s the difference between a wiggle and a straight line? Well we all know how a straight line feels, right? Rigid, unyielding, inflexible, linear. Like a Roman road or the hand of a clock. It's set, it's certain. But the wiggle, on the other hand, is soft and flexible and fluid. The wiggle is smooth and constantly in motion, right? So where the straight line is firm and brittle, the wiggle is supple and resilient -- like water -- constantly changing shape, but stronger than almost anything. As the great Alan Watts used to say, there are no straight lines in nature.

Now I've learned many of the principles of wiggledom through the process of making music because music is inherently wiggly. Music is made out of a bunch of those things, there. Essentially, music is just wiggling air. That's what's going on with music. And as musicians, we are constantly oscillating between different states, right? So high to low Or loud to quiet. Thick to thin. Music is constantly in motion. And everything in music is learned through play.

Now there are three essential types of wiggle in music that I'd like to talk to you about today. The first is called melody, what we call melody. Now a melody draws a line from one place to another and tells a story as it goes. So Louis Armstrong walks down the street, looks around and he goes, "I see trees of green." Yeah? Not, "I see trees of green." Not that. "I see trees of green." It's a tree. "I see skies are blue." It's the sky, right? "Clouds are white," there's a little cloud up there. "The bright blessed day, The dark sacred night." Is that not the sun going down? It is. A good melody arc tells a story and draws a line that moves us. That's the first kind of wiggle.

Now the second kind of wiggle is what they call rhythm. Now rhythm is about time, but it's also about the body. So Louis does not sing this: "I see trees of green. Red roses too, I see --" No, sir. Instead he goes, "I see trees green."

(Vocalizing) Right? I just saw a bunch of you do this. Rhythm physically moves the body. And with that motion and play, the melody has something to be in conversation with. And suddenly we have space, and we have form, and we have proportion and dynamics and that kind of storytelling. It's beautiful. So rhythm moves us and our melody through time. That's the second kind of wiggle.

Now the third kind of wiggle is my personal favorite, and it's what they call harmony. Now harmony is about relationships. It's the wiggles between the wiggles. And by adding these chords, little combinations of notes, like clusters of notes, we get to take our melody and our rhythm and decide how we want these things to feel. OK, so with this song, we start home. We begin home, right? Begin to move. Somewhere close by, quite warm. A bit of darkness there. Lightening. Saddening. And then something extraordinary happens. Our melody note stays the same. "And I think to myself," right, one melody note. But the chord, which could happily stay here, becomes this. "And I think to myself," did you feel the wiggle? It's special, isn't it? This note just completely changed color. Didn't it? That's the power of harmony. So with a chord, I can squint, I can reassure, I can enchant, I can purify, I can terrify. So that when I get home, in the end ... It’s all the more beautiful because we’ve traveled somewhere new. Harmony tells an emotional story through tension, release, dissonance and consonance by combining many different notes together. That's the third wiggle.

So you may say, “But Jacob, why does it make us wiggle so? How do these notes make us feel these things?” And I would say, well, because music is about so much more than just notes. Music is about life. In music, we learn that being in harmony with the world doesn't mean everyone is singing the same note at the same time. It's about embracing the dissonance and following the heart to home. We learn that being in time with the world doesn't have to mean stepping into line. It's about motion and knowing when your time is right. Leaving space for the rest. We learn that being in tune is not about being perfect. It's about following a line and being open to where it might take you. Because here's the truth of it. Life does not work in straight lines. Life is full of curveballs, full of ups and downs. And either we yield and we bend and we soften. Or we stiffen up and we break. So when the world feels like a straight line, be a wiggler. It's in your nature, trust me. You already know how to wiggle. You just need to remember.
